blogs.title: The Commissioner’s Penalty Monopoly: Eighth Circuit Narrows Private Remedies Under Minnesota’s Payment of Wages Act
blogs.description: The Eighth Circuit held that only the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry’s Commissioner—not private plaintiffs—may seek average daily wage penalties under MPWA § 181.101. Anchored in the statute’s text and structure, the court contrasted § 181.101’s commissioner-centric penalty language with neighboring provisions (§§ 181.13, 181.14) that expressly authorize employees to recover penalties themselves. This post unpacks the court’s textual analysis, the reliance on cases like Allan and Hull, and what this means for private wage-and-hour litigation strategies in Minnesota. It also considers whether plaintiffs should pair MPWA wage claims with administrative penalty pursuits and what legislative fixes might look like if the Legislature wants private penalty enforcement.

blogs.title: Civil Penalties and Article III in Wage-and-Hour Cases: Laidlaw’s Shadow over MFLSA Enforcement
blogs.description: Although Cohen stipulated he’d been paid all overtime and liquidated damages under the MFLSA, he pressed on for statutory penalties—payable to the state. The Eighth Circuit vacated and remanded for a jurisdictional inquiry, flagging potential mootness if the allegedly unlawful overtime policy has ended and is not reasonably likely to recur, while noting voluntary cessation does not automatically moot a case. This post analyzes the Laidlaw framework, Town of Chester’s claim-specific standing, and what factual record the district court needs on remand about Consilio’s current policy. It also engages with Judge Kobes’s concurrence questioning whether Laidlaw’s rationale maps neatly onto MFLSA penalties, and offers practice tips for preserving standing when the defendant tenders full wages mid-case.

blogs.title: Waiver by Under-briefing: The Demise of the MWTA Claim and Lessons for Plaintiffs
blogs.description: Cohen’s Minnesota Wage Theft Act theory—centered on deficient notice of the overtime policy change—failed not on the merits but for lack of developed argument and statutory support for private penalties. After stipulating he received all owed wages, Cohen offered “little to no” briefing and pointed to no provision authorizing civil penalties in a private MWTA suit. This post explains how issue preservation and remedy identification are outcome determinative on appeal, why MWTA § 181.032 largely channels penalties through the Commissioner, and how plaintiffs can structure MWTA claims to survive summary judgment and appellate review.

blogs.title: Pleadings Matter: Why Cohen’s Late-Breaking Injunctive Theory Went Nowhere
blogs.description: Cohen pivoted at summary judgment to seek an order rescinding Consilio’s overtime policy, but the Eighth Circuit refused to consider relief not pleaded, citing the rule that new claims must be added by amending the complaint. This post examines the hazards of shifting remedial theories at the summary judgment stage, the InfoDeli/Rule 15 lesson, and how to align injunctive requests with evolving facts without forfeiting them. It also explains how injunctive relief can be crucial to avoiding mootness in wage cases after tender, underscoring why plaintiffs should plead forward-looking remedies from the outset.
